# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Recommend a simple low budget movie that surprised you at how good it was...

**Score:** 60
**Body:** I recently watched that Rainn Wilson paramedic comedy *Code 3 (2025)* and it had no business being that good. Now I'm curious about other low budget gems... 

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Primer (2004)
2. Coherence (2013) gets mentioned on here quite a bit for good reason.

Moon (2009) felt like a miracle for $5 mil. But if you're looking for <$1 mil., I'm fond of Tangerine (2015).
3. *The Man from Earth* (2007) is a classic example of this, $200k, 8-9 days shooting. Whole movie is just one good conversation, looks like a mid 80s TV movie because it was all shot on handi-cams and they can't upscale it.

*Upgrade* (2018), fantastic sci-fi budget of only $3 million

*Cube* (1997) was made for only about $350,000
4. Timecrimes (2007)
5. The raid. Shockingly low budget for how well it was made. 
6. Short Term 12 (2013)  
Budget: $400K  
Brie Larson, Lakeith Stanfield. Rami Malek, John Gallagher Jr., Kaitlyn Dever
7. The Vast of Night (2019)
8. Blue Ruin (2013)
9. Smoke signals 1998
10. The Blair Witch Project is pretty low budget but it has an amazing atmosphere. Coherence is another gem, if you are into time travel movies.

**Score:** 24

Any language and era is fine as long as the movie is good.

1. The Man from Earth

Primer

## 4. Requesting a coastal & foggy horror/thriller

**Score:** 21
**Body:** Preferably with a lot of rain and such. I want it set in todays world (80s up until today) so nothing that takes place in the 1800s etc.

I’m thinking The Fog meets Jaws meets The Mist meets Prisoner if that makes sense. If there’s no horrors or thrillers that comes to mind then I guess dramas are okay too, think a todays version of The Banshees Of Inisherin.

Any suggestions are greatly appreciated! 

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Widow’s Bay
  - Yes! 100%. OP request fits Widow's Bay almost exactly.
2. The Lighthouse
3. Somebody's gotta say Dagon
4. A lot of Stephen King of course, I'd say Storm of the Century 
5. Okay I don’t recall that there’s any RAIN, but Insomnia has that cold, foggy vibe. Set in Alaska. 
6. Cold Skin might be exactly what youre after. Remote coastal setting, fog, rain, creature horror. Its from 2017 so it fits the era you want.

Dead And Buried

## 5. what’s a horror movie so bad it’s good? or like one that’s so bad it’s funny

**Score:** 14
**Body:** i’m not talking about movies that are obviously satire, i mean movies that try to be scary but just end up being funny or movies that are so bad and cringe that it’s good. i just need a good laugh lol

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Troll 2

## 2. Name a film whose premise sounds blah, but is a great movie.

**Score:** 837
**Body:** Name a film whose premise sounds like it would not make for a good movie, but turns out to be incredible.  The bigger the discrepancy, the better. If you told me there was a movie being made about the founder of Facebook, Mark Zuckerberg, I would not rush out to see it. The Social Network goes to show how a well-told story, tight script, and strong direction and acting can make all the difference. 

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

## 3. What is the movie monster that scares you the most to this day?

**Score:** 412
**Body:** Mine is Aragog from the Harry Potter movies, specifically his first appearance in Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets. The fact that he initially cooperates with Harry and Ron and speaks to them so calmly doesn't immediately give you the feeling that they're walking into a trap. Then, all of a sudden, the tone shifts, and I get goosebumps every time.

Julian Glover's voice acting was absolutely perfect. He made the entire scene genuinely chilling, especially when Aragog reveals what is really about to happen. And that final line:

"Go? I think not! My sons and daughters do not harm Hagrid on my command. But I cannot deny them fresh meat when it wanders so willingly into our midst. Good-bye, friend of Hagrid."

That calm, almost polite delivery of "Good-bye" somehow makes it even more terrifying. It's one of those scenes where the monster doesn't need to scream or attack you himself. He just calmly tells you that you're about to be eaten. Absolutely horrifying.

Spoilers/Reasons:

>!The movie starts by Buddy following this kid around because he didn’t want to dance like the rest of the kids, he then says how he is gonna talk to this kid to “Teach him what it means to be brave” I don’t know about you guys but that would have had me checking the rating of the movie instantly then the next scene the main kid finds the other kids book in the trash covered in “Red Paint” I mean honestly if you genuinely brought your kid to this movie and got that far to then hit the bloody parts that everyone was upset that their kid seen, you missed ALL of the red flags.!<

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Since I just watched The Bride! what movies do you think do the worst job handling their core messages?

**Score:** 108
**Body:** I decided to watch Maggie Gyllenhaal's The Bride! on a slight yesterday and my jet-lagged brain keeps circling around how incredibly poorly it managed the theme of feminism, despite how loud and insistent it tries to be about it.

I guess the takeaway is about women having their voices and choices stifled by the patriarchy, but on the other hand (spoilers if anyone still cares):

\- Ida is violently and painfully possessed against her will by the ghost of Mary Shelley. This actually leads directly to her death, since it ruins her undercover operation and she's accidentally killed as the mobsters try to snap her out of it. Thanks for that, Mary Shelley.

\- As The Bride, she experiences a taste of freedom by anachronistically going clubbing, then shortly gets into trouble and has to be rescued by her man. She then follows him around for most of the movie.

\- She is continually gaslit by Frank into believing she loves him. When he's revealed to be a manipulative liar, she almost immediately forgives him without Frank having to do anything to earn it, and their dynamic doesn't change at all.

\- The often-repeated reframe of 'I'd prefer not to' used to symbolise her rebellion against the patriarchy is from Melville's Bartleby, the Scrivener. So, we're going with a male author from a work not related to feminism at all. No suitable quotes from Mary Shelley herself, or her mother, Mary Wollstonecraft, the acclaimed female rights advocate?

\- The Bride's big moment is screaming at a room she has taken hostage at gunpoint, going on about a crime boss (from Chicago, while she's hundreds of miles away in New York) and then shooting a cop by accident. This sparks a nationwide feminist movement that mostly causes a lot of property damage.

\- Penelope Cruz's detective character has a whole arc about being denied her proper position despite being the better investigator. When she does get the promotion, the first thing she does is shoo all the male cops out of the room so that the two wanted murderers can escape justice, because it's romantic or something. This is framed as another big feminist win.

Anyway, I partly wanted to dunk on this shitty movie I wasted my time with, but I was also wondering what other movies even manage to fuck their central themes up this badly?

(Sorry if this isn't right for this sub, the r/movies automod suggested it blocking this for whatever reason.)

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Tim Burton's Alice in Wonderland is a garbage movie for several reasons, but the real sticking point to me was how it really tries to deliver a moral of 'You can't escape to fantasy to help with life' at the end. Which is antithetical to 

A, The movie we just watched

B, The central theme of Alice in Wonderland as a narrative

C, Tim Burton's entire career

D, The general idea of storytelling
  - "it's ok to be different if you're pretty"
2. Conflating the way the classic film treats the Bride of Frankenstein with Mary Shelley remains the most inexplicable fucking thing.

She didn't "go far enough?" She outlined psychological concepts in a work of fiction that Freud wouldn't articulate for another fucking century. What the fuck is this movie talking about?
  - She didn't start a feminist revolution decades early, I guess??
3. This movie has taken up more space in my brain than any other movie I have seen in years. It is truly baffling on so many different levels. I just keep thinking **why?!** Why did they make the choices they made? What message did they think they were sending? Did the cast and crew know how ridiculous this would all be? 

The simple explanation is that it's a bad movie. But there are so many plot points and character decisions in direct opposition to the assumed feminist message of the movie that I keep thinking maybe that was the point? Violence and murder aren't actually helpful for achieving equality? But what the fuck does that have to do with Frankenstein? Why does the doctor at the beginning agree to make an undead sex slave? Oh God, it's back in my brain. Why did you do this to me?!
  - Yeah I think this is the new movie for my brain to turn to when I'm trying to sleep, distracting me with it's baffling choices. The previous title holder was The Creator.

Also good point on the doctor. She makes an undead sex slave and is never held accountable for it on any level. Similarly The monster duo actually did kill two policemen in cold blood alongside the more justified/defensive killings. But fuck those guys I guess.

Another thing I keep circling back to - Mary Shelley's Frankenstein; or the Modern Prometheus is a fictional book in this universe. Mary Shelley lived and died. But the Monster is... also a real guy? Was she his biographer or what?

I could let stuff like that and the dance sequences go if the movie held to a surrealist tone throughout, but it's also trying to be gritty and serious about 75% of the time.
  - Just watch Book of Henry! That will overwhelm your 'what the FUCK were they thinking' circuits so completely that you'll forget both films. Same effect as sniffing coffee beans in between sampling colognes.
4. I just watched this the other night and tried to give it a lot of grace. 

It struggled so much to understand what and which messages to send, and then proceeded to quarter-ass all 12 ideas. The detective story was so unnecessary and disjointed. Like someone get Penelope Cruz off the screen cuz I felt like she genuinely was reading her lines for the first time. 

The Brain Freeze Female Rebellion Empowerment scene went no where and was horribly executed. Felt like a last minute addition to make it clear that yea this movie is about Gwirl Power 😉 

Coming off that ballroom scene was such a joke too. It felt like Maggie G wanted to capture that feeling from Joker and The Dark Knight but it didn’t land because the scenes weren’t even saying anything! They could have been cut and nothing would’ve changed which is sad because the dances scenes were a bit cringe but at least quirky. 

The Bride realizes her afterlife and entire reason is to just serve a man. A man who lied to her continuously because he was lonely and sexually deprived. And yet decides to stay and loved him?? Not to mention the egregious SA scenes like what??? THIS is the story Mary Shelley decides to tell from the grave? THIS is why she inserts herself into her own story (this is another weird thing you aren’t supposed to question because if MS has possessed the Bride she’s literally doing it bcuz she’s in love w her own creation … ) ???

And despite its supposed empowering message The Bride is reduced to just that. The belongings of yet another man that just wants his dick sucked.
5. Just a relatively recent one that comes to mind: 

Guardians of the Galaxy vol.3 has a pretty strong message against animal cruelty, arguing that animals can suffer and feel right alongside other beings. 

Then it turns around and shrugs when a whole planet of animal-people hybrids are destroyed, and ends with Rocket leading the new Guardians team on a mission where they will...slaughter a bunch of wild animals.
6. I think you're putting too much weight behind what you feel its core message ought to have been and less behind what it's actually portraying, which is not a typical "girl power" movie, but a movie about girls stripped of power and the ways that shapes who they become, even to their own detriment, and how a system that treats them that way prevents them from becoming equals even when they're meant to be treated as such. And I say this as someone who doesn't call himself a fan of the film really, but a fan of the effort.

The way I explained it on release:

>I can't call it good, but it would be somehow worse if it was. It feels like watching someone in an anger spiral, fueled by fury in a feedback loop pushing them further and further out beyond rationality but it keeps going until it completely shakes itself apart and the pieces keep going, and then it clumsily stitches itself back together and it keeps going, and it keels over dead and it keeps going. There's a plot here, but judging the plot is like criticizing the spelling of bathroom graffiti.

>There's several moments that had me rolling my eyes and saying "ugh," but I've never seen anything quite like it. I wouldn't change a thing, but I still can't even be sure I liked it.

I suppose that also shakes out to why I don't have much to say on the question of movies undercutting their own message as well--I don't actually care much about whether a movie functions as persuasive rhetoric. The Matrix, as an example, doesn't make a convincing case to me in either of its broad philosophical directions, but it is a fantastic movie, and one that gets people thinking about a topic enough to poke holes in it, which I consider a win all around.

## 2. If I Had Legs, I'd Kick You: why I think Conan O'Brien unironically unlocks the entire film

**Score:** 59
**Body:** In *If I Had Legs I'd Kick You,* Rose Byrne's despairing mother character 'Linda' is paying to have therapy with Conan O'Brien's character essentially daily by the last act (the movie is light of exposition but you hear it in a conversation she has on the phone with her husband when he raises how much she's paying for therapy; it's also useful because until that point I'd kind of assumed she was seeing O'Brien for free as a kind of peer supervisor/colleague deal, but no, he's charging her full fees).

I've posted about this movie before but not with this perspective: O'Brien is in *very* few scenes but Mary Bronstein really leaned on him in promo, which makes sense, but also even before production -- she had this character in her mind from the point of writing. This tells me he was central to the premise's conception.

The therapist he plays, importantly, is *so* unhelpful to Linda to be actively harmful, but also, on a technical level, he gives advice that is largely 'true'. In his first scene he deflects some of her aimlessness by telling her that her problems would get smaller if she'd just get some sleep, which is true, and pushes back on her self-flagellating. But it doesn't matter because she wants *more* from him.

She describes a dream she has about him which sounds like the kind of dream you have about an inappropriate crush. He doesn't acknowledge this, he doesn't name it. In the one scene after he actually helps her practically, Conan leaves the room as Linda whispers "I love you". Does she love him, in the sense that she wants to be intimate with him, have a relationship with him? We see Linda try to deepen their relationship in multiple settings -- in the breakroom he ignores her politesse, and in sessions she tries to push his boundaries re self-disclosure (which he calls out and immediately ends their therapeutic relationship, never appearing again).

The only moment Conan shares anything about himself or his own life, it's a totally useless story about lab rats from his time in college. He has no idea Linda just caused a hamster's murder; he has no sense that what she needs from him in that moment is a real vulnerability. But Linda (Rose Byrne's performance in this scene is so good) is begging for him to stay in that moment anyway.

All of this is, by the way, very funny -- the complete disconnect between Linda's needs and what her expensive therapist gives her is hilarious. But it's also mirrored in the relationship she has with her own clients. Caroline is begging for a deeper connection with Linda that Linda pushes off constantly, resulting in an abandoned baby and a haunting by a missing client.

It's a microcosm of every aspect of Linda's life. All of her problems are solvable via her therapists' advice but the way the Western world approaches the counselling relationship can never really meet her needs. She does *everything* against the better advice of professionals, including her daughter's doctor. Without the production's insistence on painting her life as bleakly stressful her choices would seem comically counterintuitive.

But think of our title again - not literal. But if only Linda 'had legs' -- a counselling relationship that worked, a marriage that strengthened her, an experience of parenthood that sustained her, a day-to-day life that gave her joy -- she'd have her shit together (kick you). Conan's character represents the possibility of all of these things coming together for her because she (wrongly) feels she can manipulate him into being the therapist she needs if she just pays him enough. If she could *just* get a therapist who told her what to do, as she requests (but only in the way she wants to hear it) she could fix the hole in her roof and her daughter's stomach.

It's a really interesting role to insist on giving to a famous face that people don't even remotely associate with dramatic importance -- it's as if Bronstein knew he was the key to understanding why Linda was destroying everything but wanted his pop culture presence to distract us from it.

### Top 2 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I completely missed the detail that he was charging her full price, which is, indeed, hilarious. Linda is stuck in an impossible, anguishing situation that is hopefully transitory, but feels catastrophic. 

It can happen to anyone--even someone charged with helping others navigate mental health crises and I think that's the point. 

It was seeking out help within a deeply flawed system that made her situation all the more Kafkaesque. And she gave back as much as she received by being a shitty therapist herself.

The fact that the film makes all of that so amusing and terrible is a triumph
2. From what I can recall, Rose Byrne’s character was super dependent on her therapist. She was refusing to make any decisions on her own, begging him to tell her what to do. She would consistently cross boundaries (like walking over to his office when they did not have an appointment). She was constantly looking for him to rescue her. Therapists don’t rescue their clients. When a client is stuck in a mentality of helplessness, refusing to take action to enact change in their life, and outsourcing emotional regulation onto a therapist, it is exhausting. This kind of dynamic leads to compassion fatigue for the therapist. She needed to be left on her own to become uncomfortable enough to finally make a change. Meeting with him kept her comfortable enough to stay in the same distress loop. He hit his limit and realized meeting with her was causing more harm than good.

(Also have to say, he was a terrible therapist, clearly lol. He should have referred her to someone else wayyyyy before he turned so cold.)

## 3. Perfection, Lost: How the Tremors (1990) Sequels Traded Terror and Harmony for Spectacle

**Score:** 27
**Body:** Spoilers ahead for the entire Tremors franchise. If you don't know who Burt Gummer is, or why "more guns" is always the correct answer, stop reading. I envy you. Go watch the 1990 original instead; it's the better use of your time. Proceed to the sequels at your own peril.

I don't just want to gush about Tremors, though I could. I want to argue something specific:

Tremors (1990) works because it stands on two load-bearing walls, genuine terror and genuine harmony, and each sequel that follows knocks one of them down. Aftershock keeps the harmony and abandons the terror. Back to Perfection abandons both. Watch those two walls and you can see a masterpiece decay into a merely-fun B-movie franchise in real time.

**The original: terror and harmony**

Perfection, Nevada. Population 14, soon to be adjusted downward. Val McKee (Kevin Bacon) and Earl Bassett (Fred Ward) are the town's handymen, not ranchers but odd-job men, two good-looking, believably American guys who can read each other perfectly and fall completely apart the moment a well-educated young woman shows up. That woman is Rhonda LeBeck (Finn Carter), a seismology grad student, and here's the first quiet signal of what kind of movie this is: instead of belittling her fieldwork, they try to relate to it. Are their motives entirely pure? Probably not; they clearly find her attractive. But whatever, man. They're trying, and that decency beats the modern version of this scene by a mile.

That decency is the whole ethic. In true Gene Roddenberry spirit, there is no villain among the humans. Even Melvin, the town's insufferable kid, is a nuisance, never a threat. Everyone gets along. And crucially, nobody is stupid. The horror doesn't run on characters making idiotic choices so the plot can punish them; everyone does their level best with what they know. That's why the deaths land as tragedy rather than comeuppance: Edgar dead of dehydration on the electrical tower, poor Old Fred, Walter Chang swallowed whole in the middle of his own store. No one earns it. No one deserves this. Compare that to slasher logic, where death is a moral verdict on stupidity or sin, and you see how radical Tremors' generosity toward its own cast really is.

Then there's the monster, and this is where the terror lives. The film follows Stephen King's ladder in Danse Macabre (terror, then horror, then the gross-out) with real discipline. The graboid is withheld, then glimpsed, then finally understood, and the genius of the design is that it weaponizes the one surface you cannot avoid: the ground itself is hunting you. That's an elemental, primal fear. Better still, the creatures learn. Every trick the humans invent, the graboids adapt to. These are old, patient, intelligent things, and the escalation is watching them out-think people who are themselves being clever.

Underneath the creature feature is a Western. An isolated frontier town, a siege, and salvation earned through self-reliance and pooled competence: pole-vaulting across boulders, the bulldozer, the pipe bombs, and finally luring the last worm off a cliff. It's competence porn with a heart. I wanted every single character to make it out.

**Tremors II: Aftershock (harmony survives, terror does not)**

The opening still delivers exactly what it should: an oil-field worker taken from below, down he goes. A proper graboid execution, and a clean way to onboard new "grabbies" who never saw the first film. From there it's a slow burn, and the burn is where the movie earns its keep.

Earl is the lead now. Val (Bacon) is gone, married to Rhonda, living happily off-screen. And Earl? He blew his fifteen minutes and his fortune on a failed ostrich ranch. This is the duality-of-man beat, and it's the most relatable thing in the film: the two men who survived the impossible took the two most human roads afterward. One settled down. The other squandered it, got bitter, and went stale. Then Grady Hoover, a young hustler and self-professed fan, drags Earl back in with a number: $50,000 per graboid, double if you bring one back alive. In 1996 dollars, a single confirmed kill is life-changing money, and that economic realism is doing genuine character work, not just moving the plot.

The formula does start to show. Kate Reilly, the age-appropriate geologist love interest, mirrors Rhonda a little too neatly: brilliant, attractive, conveniently single, never made the time to date. She's a beat more than a person.

But the real fork in the road is the Shriekers. The graboids metamorphose into smaller, bipedal, pack-hunting things that "see" by heat and reproduce asexually: feed one, get two. On paper: terrifying. In practice, it's the Jurassic Park move. The franchise watched velociraptors clean up and thought, let's do graboid raptors. And here's the problem with that trade: the graboid's whole genius was that it took away the ground. The Shrieker gives the ground back. It's above the surface, it's visible, and the moment you learn it hunts heat, you know how to beat it. The unknowable becomes a puzzle. Terror becomes an action set-piece. That's the actual reason the tone flips from horror to comedy-horror, not because the jokes got funnier, but because there's nothing left to dread. You feel it in the tonal whiplash of being surrounded by monsters while a cheery country-western montage plays over the hunt.

And yet the second wall holds. Everyone still gets along. Grady is grating, sure, but he's an ally you're meant to root for, not a fault line running through the town. Burt Gummer becomes the spine of the film: the survivalist who is simultaneously the most likely person to live and the reason anyone else does, whose arrogance and nonchalance double as the comic relief. The sequence of Burt trapped with the Shriekers is the movie at its best. The bond is intact even as the fear drains out of the room. Aftershock loses terror but keeps harmony, and that's exactly why it's still a good time.

**Tremors 3: Back to Perfection (both walls fall)**

First, the title, because it matters on this sub: it's Back to Perfection (2001), not "Return to."

The nostalgia is real and mostly earned. Chang's Market is now run by Jodi Chang, Walter's niece, a genuinely likeable businesswoman and a lovely nod. Nancy and Mindy Sterngood are back from the original. And El Blanco, the sterile albino graboid the town semi-adopts as a protected mascot, is a legitimately clever piece of world-building.

But this is the first film in the franchise that manufactures people you're supposed to dislike, and internal friction to go with them:

Jack ("Desert Jack"), running staged Graboid-attack tours off a catastrophe he was never there for. Pure parasite, and the film knows it. (I spent his introduction quietly rooting for the worms. Possibly a me problem. Possibly not.)

Melvin Plug returns, the town's obnoxious kid now grown into a smug real-estate developer trying to pave Perfection. The nuisance has matured into the threat.

Mindy, flanderized into "a teenager," and I mean that as a personality, not an age. She had maybe three lines in the original, so there was no real character to betray, but the vacuum gets filled with attitude and a crush on Jack that I do not buy for one second.

This is the Deep Space Nine move: deliberately seeding rifts among your own people to generate drama. On DS9 it was a bold, largely successful reinvention. Here it's a mistake, because harmony was never incidental to Tremors; it was half the machine. The instant some townsfolk become people you'd cheerfully watch get eaten, the "no one deserves this" contract is void, and the film's soul goes out with it.

One accidental grace note is buried in all of this. Mindy is played in both films by Ariana Richards, who between them played Lex in Jurassic Park. So the franchise that spent an entire sequel chasing Spielberg's velociraptors had one of his kids sitting in its own cast the whole time. Nobody could have planned it, and it's funnier than anything the movie does on purpose.

Meanwhile the creature escalation runs on autopilot. Shriekers return, then evolve into Ass-Blasters: Shriekers that gorge, ignite their own gas, and fly. Every sequel now owes you a new monster tier, and every tier drags the series further from the one idea that ever mattered: a thing beneath your feet that you cannot see.

**The Gummer Show, and the road not taken**

So why did it go this way? Follow the enthusiasm. Michael Gross has appeared in all seven films and the TV series, the only original-cast member to go the distance. When producers floated ending it at seven, he shrugged and said the door was still open, and his position is blunt: as long as the movies keep making money, he is glad to keep making them. He's the franchise's engine and its truest believer, now in his late seventies and still openly campaigning for more. Of course the series reorganized itself around Burt, and Burt is firepower, action, and fun, not dread. The repeated attempts to pass the torch to his son Travis (Jamie Kennedy, films 5 and 6) only confirm the model: this became an action-comedy about a gun guy and his legacy.

Picture the other timeline. Bacon stays. Someone leans into the terror instead of the arsenal. Seven films and a prestige HBO series that treat the graboids as a genuinely ancient, unknowable intelligence and Perfection as a town under permanent elemental siege. That Tremors doesn't exist. We got the Gummer Show instead: a genuinely good hang, sprawling now across a prequel (1889, Hiram Gummer), South Africa, the Canadian Arctic, and a tropical island.

I love the first film without a single reservation. I like the second one a great deal, for exactly what it is. The third is where you can feel the franchise decide what it's going to be, and it picks spectacle and spite over terror and harmony.

More guns really is the answer to a Shrieker.

It was never the answer to a graboid. The graboid was the answer to us.
